newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to consult with Canada over wheat trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to consult with Canada over wheat trade.

text.p: The United States intends to consult with Canada over potential grain problems before imports from Canada reach disruptive levels, U.S. trade and agriculture officials said Tuesday.

The U.S. will request these consultations at six-, nine- and 11-month intervals if Canadian durum or other wheat exceed the share of the U.S. market set under a memorandum of understanding that expired a year ago, the two agencies said.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky and Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman made the announcement in a joint statement marking the anniversary of the Sept 11 expiration of the Memorandum of Understanding.
High grain prices in the year since the MOU expired have kept Canadian grain exports to the United States much lower than the 1994/95 period.
"Following consultations, the administration will use appropriate U.S. trade laws if it appears likely that market disruption will occur," the statement said.
In monitoring the grain trade over the next 12 months, the United States will use the tariff rate quotas that were in place under the memorandum of understanding as a point of reference, it said.
The U.S. will continue to monitor the volume of barley imports from Canada, and will consider appropriate action if levels grow significantly from 1993/94 levels, it added.
Barshefsky and Glickman also said they remained concerned about the non-transparent pricing practices of the Canadian Wheat Board.

Lawmakers from U.S. Northern Plains states have asked the U.S. administration to impose numerical limits on wheat imports from Canada, but Deputy Agriculture Secretary Richard Rominger declined to say if a cap had been set.
